{{Short description|Type of ordinary differential equation}}
{{technical|date=May 2025}}
In mathematics, a [[differential equation]] is called '''Darboux differential equation''' if it satisfies the form

<math>M(x, y) dx - L(x, y) dy + N(x, y) (x dy - y dx) = 0</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Ince |first=Edward Lindsay |title=Ordinary differential equations |date=1956 |publisher=Dover |isbn=978-0-486-60349-0 |series=Dover books on advanced mathematics |location=New York |pages=29–32 |language=en}}</ref>

where <math>M(x, y)</math>, <math>L(x, y)</math> and <math>N(x, y)</math> are polynomials of <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>.

The [[Ordinary differential equation|explicit]] form of this equation is

<math>y'(x) = \frac {y N(x, y) - M(x, y)} {x N(x, y) - L(x, y)}</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Darboux equation - Encyclopedia of Mathematics |url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Darboux_equation |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=encyclopediaofmath.org}}</ref>

which, compared to the aforementioned form, may also include [[Equilibrium point (mathematics)|equillibrium points]], which must satisfy the following:

<math>\begin{cases} 
y L(x, y) - x M(x, y) = 0 \\
L = x N(x, y)
\end{cases}</math>

== The solution ==

=== General case ===
Source:<ref name=":0" />

Since the Darboux equation is effectively the gereralization of the [[Riccati equation]], the solution to it, generally speaking, cannot be found in quadratures. Darboux equation can be solved in very specific cases where certain amount of [[Particular solution|particular]] irreducable polynomial solutions <math>\check{P}_{i}(x, y)</math>, <math>1 \leqslant i \leqslant p</math> are found. Let <math>m = \max(\deg M, \deg L, \deg N)</math>.

==== Case 1. ====
If <math>p \geqslant \frac {1} {2} m (m + 1) + 2</math>, the general solution has the form of <math>u(x, y) = C</math>, where <math>u(x, y) = \prod_{i=1}^p {g(x, y, z)^{\alpha_{i}}}</math>, <math>g_{i}(x, y, z) = \check{P}_{i}\left( \frac {x} {z}, \frac {y} {z} \right) z^{\deg \check{P}_{i}} </math>, <math>\alpha_{i}</math> are constants to be determined and variable <math>z</math> in this product vanishes.

==== Case 2. ====
If <math>p = \frac {1} {2} m (m + 1) + 1</math>, given Darboux equation allows the [[integrating factor]] to be found. This factor has the exact form, as the <math>u(x, y)</math> above.

=== Homogenous case. ===
If three polynomials <math>M(x, y)</math>, <math>L(x, y)</math> and <math>N(x, y)</math> happen to be [[Homogeneous polynomial|homogenous]] and <math>M(x, y)</math> with <math>L(x, y)</math> are of the same degree, the exact solution can be expressed and found in quadratures.<ref name=":1" />

Denote <math>\deg M = \deg L = k </math>, <math>\deg N = n  </math>. 

Case, where <math>k - n = 1 </math>, makes whole equation [[Homogeneous differential equation|homogenous]].

In any other situation substituting <math>y(x) = x t(x) </math> leads to the equation of [[Bernoulli differential equation|Bernoulli]] type over the [[inverse function]] <math>x = x(t)</math>.

Since <math>M(x, y)</math>, <math>L(x, y)</math> and <math>N(x, y)</math> are homogenous with degrees <math>k  </math>, <math>k  </math> and <math>n  </math> respectively, there exist polynomials <math>\mu(t)  </math>, <math>\lambda(t)  </math> and <math>\nu(t)   </math>, such as

<math>M(x, y) = x^{k} \mu\left(\frac {y} {x}\right) = x^{k} \mu(t) </math>, <math>L(x, y) = x^{k} \lambda\left(\frac {y} {x}\right) = x^{k} \lambda(t) </math>, and <math>N(x, y) = x^{n} \nu\left(\frac {y} {x}\right) = x^{n} \nu(t)  </math>.

Putting everything together yields <math>x t'(x) = \frac {x^{n + 1} t \nu(t) - x^{k} \mu(t)} {x^{n + 1} \nu(t) - x^{k}\nu(t)} - t 
= \frac {x^{k} \big( \lambda(t) - \mu(t) \big)} {x^{n + 1} \nu(t) - x^{k} \lambda(t)}
= \frac {\lambda(t) - \mu(t)} {x^{n + 1 - k} \nu(t) - \lambda(t)}</math>.

If <math>k - n = 1 </math> the resulting equation is [[Separation of variables|separable]], while in any other case, according to the [[inverse function rule]],

<math>x'(t) + \frac {\lambda(t)} {\lambda(t) - \mu(t)} x(t) = \frac {\nu(t)} {\lambda(t) - \mu(t)} \big(x(t)\big)^{n + 2 - k}</math>.

The latter is the Bernoulli equation, which is always integrable in quadratures.

== Generalized Darboux equation ==
The differential equation is called '''generalized (homogenous) Darboux equation'''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Losev |first=Dimitry Vitalievich |date=2025-02-24 |title=Уравнения Якоби и Дарбу |trans-title=The differential equations of Jacobi and Darboux |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CJoyTxpX5Tw |access-date=2025-03-16 |website=Youtube |language=ru |type=Video}}</ref> if it has the form of

<math>\phi\left( \frac {y} {x} \right) dx + \psi \left( \frac {y} {x} \right) dy + x^{k} \chi \left( \frac {y} {x} \right) (x dy - y dx) = 0</math>

where functions <math>\phi( \frac {y} {x}) = \phi(t)   </math>, <math>\psi( \frac {y} {x}) = \psi(t)   </math> and <math>\chi( \frac {y} {x}) = \chi(t)   </math> are arbitrary.

It can be reduced to [[Bernoulli differential equation|Bernoulli equation]] by following the same approach, mentioned above. Substituting <math>y(x) = x t(x)   </math> leads to the equation

<math>\big( \phi(t) + t \psi(t) \big) dx + \big( x\psi(t) + x^{k + 2} \chi(t) \big) dt = 0</math>

or in the explicit form

<math>x'(t) + \frac {\psi(t)} {\phi(t) + t \psi(t)} x(t) + \frac {\chi(t)} {\phi(t) + t \psi(t)} \big(x(t)\big)^{k + 2} = 0   </math>

which is either separable if <math>k = -2 </math>, or the Bernoulli equation over <math>x = x(t) </math> otherwise.
